title: THE WHALE THAT CARRIED A WEATHER FRONT
deck: A storm-bearing whale the length of a town has followed her seam inland, burying the barley that feeds half a continent in a winter it was never meant to see. Illuminara has four days, a pilot who will not whistle at a grandmother, a port that will not close, and a pressure trace nobody has read as a breath.
shape: Five scenes across four days: a track laid over the wrong map, a stack switched off to prove or break a theory, a margin note that turns noise into breath, a bend that fails because two edges compete, and a toll paid on the quay.

scenes.title: The Wrong Winter
paragraphs: *Karsk Harbour Control · Day One, 05:40*

Snow was falling on barley that had never met it. Sixty kilometres inland the Hallow Plains lay under a cloud that did not move with the wind, because it was not weather. It was cargo. Orrow carried it in the hollow behind her body, a storm the length of a town, and for the first time in living memory she was carrying it the wrong way.

Dov Aranda stood at the harbour window with his back to the room. Ten waste-heat stacks ran along the Karsk breakwater, each breathing the furnaces' warmth into the dark, and forty thousand jobs hung from them like washing.

**Tomas Reeve**  
The barley flowers next week. Two hard nights and the Plains lose a year. I'm asking for the whistles. Sonic herding, today, and she turns round.

**Marit Ilves**  
My family has kept this coast's snow for nine generations and not one of us ever whistled at her. You don't herd something that size. You frighten it, and a frightened thing that size doesn't turn. It falls.

**Dov Aranda**  
And I am not closing the port over a theory about a whale.
Illuminara had said nothing since she arrived. She had the pressure logs open on the long table, fourteen months of them, and beside them a hand-written logbook that smelled of salt and lamp oil.

**Illuminara**  
Nobody has said she is lost. A lost thing wanders, and she hasn't. Don't show me her track on the coast map. Show me the temperature map.

The overlay took Marit's clerk two minutes. Orrow's track lay across it like a thread laid along a crease. It followed exactly the line where the sea's cold air met the land's warm, and eleven months ago that line had bent inland, away from the breakwater, the way a tablecloth bends when someone pushes it from one side.

**Marit Ilves**  
The seam. Our book calls it the seam. She rides it. She has always ridden it.

**Illuminara**  
Then she hasn't chosen to leave the coast. The coast moved. Mr. Aranda, your ten stacks put a warm plume over the shore the size of a county, and that plume has pushed the seam inland. She is following it faithfully into the barley.

**Dov Aranda**  
That is a story. I would like a measurement.

**Illuminara**  
Good. Then let me give you a way to prove me wrong.

scenes.title: One Stack
paragraphs: *Karsk Port, Stack Seven · Day One, 14:20*

She asked for the smallest thing that could embarrass her. Stack Seven, the one nearest the sea, cold for twenty-five minutes. That would cost the port a berth: the Marigold Anne would swing at anchor, and her demurrage ran to eleven thousand a day.

**Illuminara**  
When Seven goes dark, the seam at the Gull Stone buoy should slide about four kilometres seaward within ninety minutes, and creep back after you relight it. If it doesn't move, I have been talking nonsense and you may say so in public.

**Dov Aranda**  
You would say so yourself?

**Illuminara**  
I would say so first.
Ines Calder, who spoke for the crane crews and trusted nothing that came from an office, looked at the sea and then at her director.

**Ines Calder**  
Twenty-five minutes, Dov. I've lost more to a bad tide table.

He closed Seven at 14:41. The furnace vented through its bypass with a noise like a struck bell, and the deck went quiet in the way a room does when a stranger has just said something true. At 15:06 he relit the stack. Nobody left.
At 16:05 the buoy reported the seam four point three kilometres out. At 17:20 it was home again, right to the decimetre.

Aboard the survey glider, sixty kilometres inland, the lidar caught something smaller. Orrow's great bow had come round one and a half degrees toward the sea and held there until the seam slid back. Nobody on the deck said anything.

**Tomas Reeve**  
She heard it. For ninety minutes she heard it.

**Dov Aranda**  
Fine. It's the stacks. Now tell me what a man is supposed to do with ten of them.

scenes.title: The Six Days
paragraphs: *Gull Stone Light, the pilots' house · Day Two, 07:10*

Illuminara's plan fitted on one page. Ten stacks, each with a heat exchanger that could run backward, turned from furnaces' chimneys into evaporative chillers. Lit in a line from the port out to sea, they would raise a cold shoulder across the warm plume: a second seam, steeper than the old one, bending gently toward open water. The whale would not be pushed. She would simply find the stronger edge, and an edge was the only thing she had ever followed.

**Illuminara**  
A bend of one degree for every four kilometres. Anything sharper reads as a wall. I'd light the first tower at noon tomorrow.

**Marit Ilves**  
Not at noon.
Marit had the old logbook open at a page softened by a century of thumbs. She did not look at the numbers. She looked at the margin.

**Marit Ilves**  
Orrow turns on the out-breath. Never the in. My great-grandmother wrote it twelve times, in the margin, like a prayer. If your bend arrives while she's breathing in, she'll stall, and the storm will spill wherever she stops.
Illuminara went back to the pressure trace and sat very still. The sawtooth she had marked as noise on Day One rose for twenty-six minutes and fell for twelve, over and over, fourteen months deep.

**Illuminara**  
That is not noise. That is her lungs. I filed your whale's breathing under static.

**Marit Ilves**  
Most people do.

**Illuminara**  
The bend has to arrive in the twelve-minute fall. If you tell me when she exhales, I can time the towers to it.

**Dov Aranda**  
One stack moved the seam four point three kilometres in ninety minutes. If the edge moves that fast, why did ten stacks need eleven months to carry it sixty kilometres inland?

**Illuminara**  
Because an edge answers a sudden heat change quickly; the stored heat of the shore and the route Orrow has learned accumulate slowly. We are steering one passage, not undoing eleven months of climate in a day. The exchangers already reverse for condenser cleaning. What costs time is cooling the furnaces and bringing them back without cracking them.

**Dov Aranda**  
And what does the port pay for this? Six idle days means six days of no ore, no wages and a ship fine for every berth.

**Ines Calder**  
Wages for every crane hand, full pay, every closed day. Put it on paper or the crews lift their own hands from the levers.

**Marit Ilves**  
And the coast council signs your second-phase licence. With the six days written into it.
Dov looked from one woman to the other. He had come to the room expecting to defend a harbour. He was being asked, instead, to take on a tide.

**Dov Aranda**  
One migration. Next autumn we repeat the one-stack test before the licence renews. If the measured seam is not off its old line, the six days do not trigger. If it is, full wages and all six.

**Marit Ilves**  
You may review the machinery. You do not get a review clause on whether she may pass without whistles.

**Dov Aranda**  
Agreed.
Ines took his pen before the word had finished leaving him.

scenes.title: Two Magnets
paragraphs: *Karsk estuary, survey glider · Day Three, 11:40*

They lit the chillers on Marit's count, land end first, because the land stacks were the easiest to turn and the plan said the order did not matter. At 11:52 Orrow began to exhale. Marit lifted one hand from the rail and said nothing at all.

The cold shoulder rose along the estuary tower by tower. For nine minutes the whale's bow swung toward it, exactly as the log said it would. Then it slowed, hung, and stopped, and her storm, which had always travelled behind her, rolled forward onto the port in a single wall of snow.

The cranes were already lying flat. Nothing was broken. For four hours the quay went white, the Marigold Anne became a rumour in the weather, and Dov Aranda watched his furnaces cool on the instrument panel with his fists in his pockets.

**Dov Aranda**  
You had her turning.

**Marit Ilves**  
She's afraid of something.

**Illuminara**  
Not afraid. Look at her call.
On the trace, the whale's long tone rose, jumped sideways, rose again, and jumped back, like a compass needle held between two magnets.

**Illuminara**  
At 11:52, which edge steepened first?

Tomas pulled the shore-temperature trace beneath the call. The cold line had formed inland while the sea-end stacks were still warm. For nine minutes the new line won. Then the unchanged breakwater plume sharpened the old seam nearer Orrow's bow.

**Tomas Reeve**  
The land towers gave her a new edge, but we left the old one standing at the sea end. When it became steeper, she turned back to it.

**Illuminara**  
Two edges, then. I was moving a line when I should have been controlling which line was steeper, and when.

**Marit Ilves**  
Then light the sea end first.

**Illuminara**  
Sea end first, so the seaward edge is already the steepest one she can reach. Then step the land stacks down only on her out-breath, before the old edge can sharpen behind her. Marit, how long between towers?
Marit counted on her fingers against the old rhythm of the tide.

**Marit Ilves**  
Eleven minutes. Not eight. She doesn't like to be hurried through a door.

**Dov Aranda**  
Tomorrow, then. And the Plains?

**Tomas Reeve**  
Eight thousand hectares froze last night. If she isn't turned by tomorrow night, we lose another twenty.

scenes.title: The Toll
paragraphs: *Karsk quay · Day Four, 19:30*

By evening every crane stood folded and the quay was crowded with people who did not need to be there: pilots, furnace men, schoolchildren on their parents' shoulders, Ines Calder with her arms folded and her eyes on the sky.

At 19:34 Orrow exhaled. The sea-end tower lit before the sound of her breath had reached the harbour. The next followed eleven minutes after it, and the next. Along the estuary the cold shoulder climbed out toward the open water in a line as clean as a drawn string, while behind it, tower by tower, the land stacks stepped down into silence.

She came down the estuary at six hundred metres, so close that the shadow of her passing lay across the water for a long while after she was gone. She was the colour of old pewter. Her storm trailed behind her, wide as a province, and her bow was steady on the new seam, and she did not stall.

The model put her across the breakwater on the next out-breath. Instead she held station for thirteen minutes beyond it. On the thermal map, the closest cold ground lay beneath the sea-end chiller court beside the crew shelters; the vacant eastern apron was six degrees warmer. Orrow crossed the colder pocket and shifted three body-lengths east, away from the housing roofs and the shelters.

Only then did she empty the hollow behind her. Snow struck the idle stacks and the vacant loading apron hard enough to hide them, while the lit windows behind the seawall remained dark shapes in clear air.

**Marit Ilves**  
She placed it.
Orrow turned along the edge she had always followed. The snow went on falling over the empty quay after she had passed, a toll laid where the port could bear it.

**Tomas Reeve**  
Control, this is the Plains. The wind has swung. We are getting sleet on the east fields, not snow. The frost front is holding a hundred kilometres out. The eight thousand that froze are gone. We are keeping forty-one thousand hectares of flowering barley.

**Dov Aranda**  
Ines. Stand the crews down. Full wages, all six days.

**Ines Calder**  
You can say it quieter. The whole quay heard.

Marit sat on a bollard with the logbook open on her knee and turned to a clean page. She wrote the date in the old fashion, and then, below it, in a hand that shook a little from the cold: the stacks, the order of the towers, the eleven minutes, the out-breath, and the thirteen minutes Orrow had kept for herself.

**Marit Ilves**  
I thought she'd be here to tell me it would hold.

**Illuminara**  
It won't, not on its own. The seam moves with the ice, and next autumn the ice will have moved. Someone will have to learn her again. I would start with her breath.

**Marit Ilves**  
I'd start with the margin.
Snow settled on the idle stacks and on the folded cranes. Along the breakwater, one by one, the chillers went dark, and the port, which had given up six days for a whale, began counting them down.

critic_line: A storm-bearing whale the length of a town is turned by a port that learns to read a temperature map, and the one thing nobody designed is where she chooses to lay her snow.

translation_sl.title: KIT, KI JE NOSIL VREMENSKO FRONTO
translation_sl.deck: Kit z viharjem, dolgim kakor mesto, je sledil svojemu šivu v notranjost in ječmen, ki hrani polovico celine, pokopal pod zimo, kakršne ne bi smel nikoli doživeti. Illuminara ima štiri dni, pilotko, ki ne bo zažvižgala babici, pristanišče, ki se noče zapreti, in zapis tlaka, ki ga nihče ni prebral kot dihanje.
translation_sl.shape: Pet prizorov v štirih dneh: sled, položena čez napačen zemljevid; dimnik, ugasnjen, da teorijo dokaže ali ovrže; opomba ob robu, ki šum spremeni v dihanje; upogib, ki spodleti, ker tekmujeta dva robova; in davek, plačan na pomolu.

scenes.title: Napačna zima
paragraphs: *Nadzorna soba pristanišča Karsk · Prvi dan, 05:40*

Sneg je padal na ječmen, ki ga še nikoli ni srečal. Šestdeset kilometrov v notranjosti so Hallow Plains ležale pod oblakom, ki se ni premikal z vetrom, ker ni bil vreme. Bil je tovor. Orrow ga je nosila v vdolbini za svojim telesom, vihar dolg kakor mesto, in prvič, odkar je segal živ spomin, ga je nosila v napačno smer.

Dov Aranda je stal ob pristaniškem oknu s hrbtom proti sobi. Vzdolž valobrana Karsk je teklo deset dimnikov za odvečno toploto, vsak je izdihoval toploto peči v temo, z njih pa je kakor perilo viselo štirideset tisoč delovnih mest.

**Tomas Reeve**  
Ječmen bo zacvetel naslednji teden. Dve ostri noči in Planjave izgubijo leto. Zahtevam piščali. Zvočno usmerjanje, še danes, in obrnila se bo.

**Marit Ilves**  
Moja družina devet rodov varuje sneg te obale in niti eden izmed nas ji ni nikoli zažvižgal. Ne usmerjaš nečesa tako velikega. Prestrašiš ga, prestrašena stvar te velikosti pa se ne obrne. Pade.

**Dov Aranda**  
In jaz pristanišča ne bom zaprl zaradi teorije o kitu.

Illuminara ni rekla ničesar, odkar je prispela. Na dolgi mizi je imela odprte dnevnike tlaka, štirinajst mesecev podatkov, ob njih pa ročno pisano ladijsko knjigo, ki je dišala po soli in olju za svetilke.

**Illuminara**  
Nihče ni rekel, da se je izgubila. Izgubljeno bitje tava, ona pa ni. Ne kažite mi njene sledi na zemljevidu obale. Pokažite mi zemljevid temperatur.

Maritina uradnica je za prekrivanje zemljevidov potrebovala dve minuti. Orrowina sled je ležala čeznj kakor nit vzdolž pregiba. Natanko je sledila črti, kjer se je hladni morski zrak srečal s toplim kopenskim, pred enajstimi meseci pa se je ta črta upognila v notranjost, stran od valobrana, kakor se namizni prt upogne, ko ga nekdo potisne z ene strani.

**Marit Ilves**  
Šiv. Naša knjiga mu pravi šiv. Po njem jezdi. Vedno je jezdila po njem.

**Illuminara**  
Potem se ni odločila zapustiti obale. Obala se je premaknila. Gospod Aranda, vaših deset dimnikov je nad obalo položilo topel tok, velik kakor okrožje, in ta tok je šiv potisnil v notranjost. Ona mu zvesto sledi v ječmen.

**Dov Aranda**  
To je zgodba. Rad bi meritev.

**Illuminara**  
Dobro. Potem naj vam dam način, da dokažete, da se motim.

scenes.title: En dimnik
paragraphs: *Pristanišče Karsk, dimnik sedem · Prvi dan, 14:20*

Prosila je za najmanjšo stvar, ki bi jo lahko osramotila. Dimnik sedem, najbližji morju, naj bo petindvajset minut hladen. Pristanišče bi to stalo enega priveza: Marigold Anne bi se zibala na sidru, njena ležarina pa je znašala enajst tisoč na dan.

**Illuminara**  
Ko sedmica ugasne, bi moral šiv pri boji Gull Stone v devetdesetih minutah zdrsniti približno štiri kilometre proti morju in se po ponovnem vžigu splaziti nazaj. Če se ne premakne, sem govorila neumnosti in to lahko poveste javno.

**Dov Aranda**  
Bi to sami povedali?

**Illuminara**  
Povedala bi prva.
Ines Calder, ki je govorila v imenu posadk žerjavov in ni zaupala ničemur, kar je prišlo iz pisarne, je pogledala morje in nato svojega direktorja.

**Ines Calder**  
Petindvajset minut, Dov. Zaradi slabe plimske tabele sem izgubila že več.

Sedmico je zaprl ob 14:41. Peč je skozi obvod odzračila z zvokom udarjenega zvona, krov pa je utihnil kakor soba, v kateri je tujec pravkar povedal nekaj resničnega. Ob 15:06 je dimnik znova prižgal. Nihče ni odšel.
Ob 16:05 je boja sporočila, da je šiv štiri cele tri kilometra zunaj. Ob 17:20 je bil spet doma, natančno do decimetra.

Na krovu raziskovalnega jadralnika, šestdeset kilometrov v notranjosti, je lidar ujel nekaj manjšega. Orrowin veliki premec se je obrnil za poldrugo stopinjo proti morju in tam ostal, dokler šiv ni zdrsnil nazaj. Nihče na krovu ni rekel ničesar.

**Tomas Reeve**  
Slišala ga je. Devetdeset minut ga je slišala.

**Dov Aranda**  
Prav. Dimniki so. Zdaj mi pa povejte, kaj naj človek naredi z desetimi.

scenes.title: Šest dni
paragraphs: *Svetilnik Gull Stone, hiša pilotov · Drugi dan, 07:10*

Illuminarin načrt je šel na eno stran. Deset dimnikov, vsak s toplotnim izmenjevalnikom, ki je lahko deloval v obratni smeri, bi se iz dimnikov peči spremenilo v izhlapevalne hladilnike. Prižgani v vrsti od pristanišča proti morju bi čez topel tok dvignili hladno ramo: drugi šiv, strmejši od starega, ki bi se nežno upognil proti odprti vodi. Kita ne bi potiskali. Preprosto bi našla močnejši rob, rob pa je bil edino, čemur je kdaj sledila.

**Illuminara**  
Upogib ene stopinje na vsake štiri kilometre. Vse ostrejše se bere kot zid. Prvi stolp bi prižgala jutri opoldne.

**Marit Ilves**  
Ne opoldne.
Marit je imela staro ladijsko knjigo odprto na strani, zmehčani od stoletja palcev. Ni gledala številk. Gledala je rob strani.

**Marit Ilves**  
Orrow se obrne ob izdihu. Nikoli ob vdihu. Moja prababica je to dvanajstkrat zapisala ob robu, kakor molitev. Če vaš upogib pride, ko vdihuje, bo obstala, vihar pa se bo razlil, kjerkoli se ustavi.

Illuminara se je vrnila k zapisu tlaka in sedla povsem pri miru. Žagasti vzorec, ki ga je prvi dan označila za šum, se je šestindvajset minut dvigal in dvanajst minut padal, znova in znova, skozi štirinajst mesecev.

**Illuminara**  
To ni šum. To so njena pljuča. Dihanje vašega kita sem uvrstila med motnje.

**Marit Ilves**  
Večina ljudi ga.

**Illuminara**  
Upogib mora priti v dvanajstminutnem padcu. Če mi poveste, kdaj izdihne, lahko stolpe časovno uskladim z njim.

**Dov Aranda**  
En dimnik je v devetdesetih minutah premaknil šiv za štiri cele tri kilometra. Če se rob premika tako hitro, zakaj je deset dimnikov potrebovalo enajst mesecev, da ga je odneslo šestdeset kilometrov v notranjost?

**Illuminara**  
Ker se rob na nenadno spremembo toplote odzove hitro, shranjena toplota obale in pot, ki se je je Orrow naučila, pa se kopičita počasi. Usmerjamo en prehod, ne odpravljamo enajstih mesecev podnebja v enem dnevu. Izmenjevalniki se že zdaj obrnejo za čiščenje kondenzatorjev. Čas terjata ohlajanje peči in njihov ponovni zagon brez razpok.

**Dov Aranda**  
In kaj pristanišče plača za to? Šest dni mirovanja pomeni šest dni brez rude, brez plač in ladijsko kazen za vsak privez.

**Ines Calder**  
Plače za vsakega žerjavista, polno plačilo za vsak dan zaprtja. Zapišite ali pa bodo posadke same umaknile roke z vzvodov.

**Marit Ilves**  
Obalni svet pa podpiše vaše dovoljenje za drugo fazo. S šestimi dnevi zapisanimi v njem.
Dov je pogledal z ene ženske na drugo. V sobo je prišel v pričakovanju, da bo branil pristanišče. Namesto tega so ga prosili, naj prevzame plimo.

**Dov Aranda**  
Ena selitev. Naslednjo jesen ponovimo preizkus z enim dimnikom, preden se dovoljenje obnovi. Če izmerjeni šiv ni odmaknjen od stare črte, se šest dni ne sproži. Če je, polne plače in vseh šest.

**Marit Ilves**  
Lahko pregledate stroje. Ne dobite pa klavzule za presojo, ali sme mimo brez piščali.

**Dov Aranda**  
Dogovorjeno.
Ines mu je vzela pero, še preden je beseda do konca zapustila njegova usta.

scenes.title: Dva magneta
paragraphs: *Ustje Karska, raziskovalni jadralnik · Tretji dan, 11:40*

Hladilnike so prižgali na Maritino štetje, najprej na kopenskem koncu, ker je bilo kopenske dimnike najlažje obrniti, načrt pa je trdil, da vrstni red ni pomemben. Ob 11:52 je Orrow začela izdihovati. Marit je dvignila eno roko z ograje in ni rekla ničesar.

Hladna rama se je vzdolž ustja dvigala stolp za stolpom. Devet minut se je kitov premec obračal proti njej, natanko tako, kot je napovedovala knjiga. Nato se je upočasnil, obvisel in obstal, njen vihar, ki je vedno potoval za njo, pa se je v enem samem snežnem zidu prevalil naprej na pristanišče.

Žerjavi so že ležali položeni. Nič se ni zlomilo. Štiri ure je bil pomol bel, Marigold Anne je postala govorica v vremenu, Dov Aranda pa je s pestmi v žepih na instrumentni plošči gledal, kako se njegove peči hladijo.

**Dov Aranda**  
Obračala se je.

**Marit Ilves**  
Nečesa se boji.

**Illuminara**  
Ne boji se. Poglejte njen klic.
Na zapisu se je kitov dolgi ton dvignil, skočil vstran, se znova dvignil in skočil nazaj, kakor igla kompasa med dvema magnetoma.

**Illuminara**  
Kateri rob je ob 11:52 postal strmejši prvi?

Tomas je pod klic potegnil zapis temperature obale. Hladna črta je nastala v notranjosti, medtem ko so bili dimniki na morskem koncu še topli. Devet minut je zmagovala nova črta. Nato je nespremenjeni topli tok valobrana izostril stari šiv bliže Orrowinemu premcu.

**Tomas Reeve**  
Kopenski stolpi so ji dali nov rob, starega na morskem koncu pa smo pustili stati. Ko je postal strmejši, se je obrnila nazaj k njemu.

**Illuminara**  
Torej dva robova. Premikala sem črto, morala pa bi nadzorovati, katera črta je strmejša in kdaj.

**Marit Ilves**  
Potem najprej prižgite morski konec.

**Illuminara**  
Najprej morski konec, da je rob proti morju že najstrmejši, ki ga lahko doseže. Nato kopenske dimnike zmanjšujte samo ob njenem izdihu, preden se lahko stari rob za njo izostri. Marit, koliko časa med stolpi?
Marit je na prste štela po starem ritmu plime.

**Marit Ilves**  
Enajst minut. Ne osem. Ne mara, da jo priganjajo skozi vrata.

**Dov Aranda**  
Torej jutri. Kaj pa Planjave?

**Tomas Reeve**  
Sinoči je zmrznilo osem tisoč hektarov. Če je do jutri zvečer ne obrnemo, jih izgubimo še dvajset.

scenes.title: Davek
paragraphs: *Pomol Karsk · Četrti dan, 19:30*
Do večera je vsak žerjav stal zložen, pomol pa je bil poln ljudi, ki jim ne bi bilo treba biti tam: pilotov, kurjačev, šolarjev na ramenih staršev, Ines Calder s prekrižanimi rokami in očmi na nebu.

Ob 19:34 je Orrow izdihnila. Stolp na morskem koncu se je prižgal, preden je zvok njenega diha dosegel pristanišče. Naslednji mu je sledil enajst minut pozneje in nato naslednji. Vzdolž ustja se je hladna rama vzpenjala proti odprti vodi po črti, čisti kakor napeta vrvica, medtem ko so za njo kopenski dimniki, stolp za stolpom, ugašali v tišino.

Po ustju je prišla na višini šeststo metrov, tako blizu, da je senca njenega prehoda še dolgo po njenem odhodu ležala čez vodo. Bila je barve starega kositra. Njen vihar se je vlekel za njo, širok kakor pokrajina, njen premec pa je mirno držal novi šiv in ni obstala.

Model jo je ob naslednjem izdihu postavil čez valobran. Namesto tega je za njim trinajst minut mirovala na mestu. Na termalnem zemljevidu so bila najbližja hladna tla pod ploščadjo hladilnikov na morskem koncu poleg zavetišč posadk; prazna vzhodna nakladalna ploščad je bila šest stopinj toplejša. Orrow je prečkala hladnejši žep in se premaknila tri telesne dolžine proti vzhodu, stran od stanovanjskih streh in zavetišč.

Šele nato je izpraznila vdolbino za seboj. Sneg je udaril po mirujočih dimnikih in prazni nakladalni ploščadi tako močno, da jih je skril, osvetljena okna za morskim zidom pa so ostala temne oblike v čistem zraku.

**Marit Ilves**  
Ona ga je položila tja.
Orrow se je obrnila vzdolž roba, ki mu je vedno sledila. Sneg je po njenem prehodu še naprej padal na prazen pomol, davek, odložen tja, kjer ga je pristanišče lahko preneslo.

**Tomas Reeve**  
Nadzorna soba, tukaj Planjave. Veter se je obrnil. Na vzhodnih poljih dobivamo sodro, ne snega. Fronta zmrzali vztraja sto kilometrov proč. Osem tisoč hektarov, ki so zmrznili, je izgubljenih. Ohranili bomo enainštirideset tisoč hektarov cvetočega ječmena.

**Dov Aranda**  
Ines. Razpusti posadke. Polne plače, vseh šest dni.

**Ines Calder**  
Lahko poveste tiše. Slišal je ves pomol.

Marit je sedela na privezniku z ladijsko knjigo odprto na kolenu in obrnila na čisto stran. Datum je zapisala po starem, pod njim pa z roko, ki se je malo tresla od mraza: dimnike, vrstni red stolpov, enajst minut, izdih in trinajst minut, ki jih je Orrow zadržala zase.

**Marit Ilves**  
Mislila sem, da bo tukaj in mi povedala, da bo držalo.

**Illuminara**  
Ne bo, ne samo od sebe. Šiv se premika z ledom, naslednjo jesen pa se bo led premaknil. Nekdo se je bo moral naučiti znova. Jaz bi začela z njenim dihom.

**Marit Ilves**  
Jaz bi začela z robom strani.
Sneg je legel na mirujoče dimnike in zložene žerjave. Vzdolž valobrana so hladilniki drug za drugim ugašali, pristanišče, ki je za kita odstopilo šest dni, pa jih je začelo odštevati.

translation_sl.critic_line: Kita z viharjem, dolgega kakor mesto, obrne pristanišče, ki se nauči brati zemljevid temperatur, edina stvar, ki je ni zasnoval nihče, pa je kraj, kamor se sama odloči položiti svoj sneg.
